Lecture 3

Symplectic manifolds

What this lecture does

Lecture 1 gave a bracket and Lecture 2 gave forms. They are the same structure, and this lecture names it: a closed, non-degenerate 222-form ω\sympω. Naming it buys three things the rest of Part I spends. Darboux’s theorem says that all the interesting content of a symplectic manifold is global, which is exactly what the Liouville–Arnold theorem of Lecture 4 exploits; Lagrangian submanifolds are the shape its invariant tori will turn out to have; and the canonical 111-form p⋅dqp\cdot\dd qp⋅dq is what the action variables of Lecture 5 are built from.

3.1 The symplectic form

Lecture 4’s first step is that a regular level set of nnn independent commuting integrals is Lagrangian (§3.6), and its difficulty is that its conclusion is global, because locally there is nothing to prove (§3.3). Lecture 5 needs p⋅dqp\cdot\dd qp⋅dq to be a genuine 111-form on phase space (§3.7) and generating functions to produce canonical transformations (§3.4). One piece of notation first: a 222-form eats two vectors, and feeding it one leaves a 111-form.

Definition 3.1 (Interior product). For a 222-form β\betaβ and a vector vvv at the same point, ιvβ\iota_v\betaιv​β is the 111-form w↦β(v,w)w\mapsto\beta(v,w)w↦β(v,w). The slot that vvv fills is the first.

Definition 3.2 (Symplectic form, symplectic manifold). A 222-form ω\sympω on a manifold M\phaseM is symplectic if

  1. it is closed: dω=0\dd\symp=0dω=0; and

  2. it is non-degenerate: at each point, if ω(v,w)=0\symp(v,w)=0ω(v,w)=0 for every www, then v=0v=0v=0.

The pair (M,ω)(\phase,\symp)(M,ω) is a symplectic manifold.

Condition 2 says that the linear map v↦ιvωv\mapsto\iota_v\sympv↦ιv​ω from TpMT_p\phaseTp​M to Tp∗MT_p^{*}\phaseTp∗​M has zero kernel. The two spaces have the same dimension, so v  ⟼  ιvωis an isomorphism TpM  →  ∼    Tp∗M. v\;\longmapsto\;\iota_v\symp \quad\text{is an isomorphism } T_p\phase\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;T_p^{*}\phase . v⟼ιv​ωis an isomorphism Tp​M∼​Tp∗​M.(3.1) A symplectic form converts vectors into covectors and back, with no choices made — the job an inner product does in Euclidean space, done by an antisymmetric object.

Example 3.3 (The standard symplectic form). On R2n\R^{2n}R2n with coordinates q1,…,qn,p1,…,pnq_1,\dots,q_n,p_1,\dots,p_nq1​,…,qn​,p1​,…,pn​, ω  =  ∑i=1ndqi∧dpi,ω(v,w)=∑i=1n(vqiwpi−vpiwqi), \symp\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}\dd q_i\wedge\dd p_i , \qquad \symp(v,w)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(v^{q_i}w^{p_i}-v^{p_i}w^{q_i}\big), ω=i=1∑n​dqi​∧dpi​,ω(v,w)=i=1∑n​(vqi​wpi​−vpi​wqi​),(3.2) by (2.5). Geometrically, ω(v,w)\symp(v,w)ω(v,w) is the sum over iii of the signed areas of the shadows of the parallelogram on v,wv,wv,w in the (qi,pi)(q_i,p_i)(qi​,pi​)-planes; for n=1n=1n=1 it is the signed area itself (Figure 3.1). It pairs each position only with its own momentum.

In matrix form, with vectors written as columns in the order (q,p)(q,p)(q,p), ω(v,w)=vTΩ w,Ω=(01n−1n0). \symp(v,w)=v^{\mathsf T}\Omega\,w, \qquad \Omega=\begin{pmatrix}0&\Id_n\\-\Id_n&0\end{pmatrix} . ω(v,w)=vTΩw,Ω=(0−1n​​1n​0​).(3.3) It is closed because its coefficients are constant, and non-degenerate because det⁡Ω=1\det\Omega=1detΩ=1.

Proposition 3.4 (Phase space has even dimension). A non-degenerate 222-form exists only on a manifold of even dimension.

Proof. At a point, write ω\sympω as an m×mm\times mm×m matrix WWW in some basis. It is antisymmetric, so det⁡W=det⁡WT=det⁡(−W)=(−1)mdet⁡W\det W=\det W^{\mathsf T}=\det(-W)=(-1)^{m}\det WdetW=detWT=det(−W)=(−1)mdetW. For mmm odd this forces det⁡W=0\det W=0detW=0, so WWW has a kernel and ω\sympω is degenerate.

Any symplectic form gives a bracket

Turn (3.6) round and make it a definition: on any symplectic manifold, put {f,g}  :=  ω(Xf,Xg)=df(Xg). \pb{f}{g}\;:=\;\symp(\hvf{f},\hvf{g})=\dd f(\hvf{g}) . {f,g}:=ω(Xf​,Xg​)=df(Xg​).(3.7) It is bilinear and antisymmetric, and satisfies Leibniz because d(fg)=f dg+g df\dd(fg)=f\,\dd g+g\,\dd fd(fg)=fdg+gdf. What is left is Jacobi, and this is where closedness enters.

3.3 Darboux’s theorem

Theorem 3.10 (Darboux sketched). Every point of a 2n2n2n-dimensional symplectic manifold (M,ω)(\phase,\symp)(M,ω) has a chart q1,…,qn,p1,…,pnq_1,\dots,q_n,p_1,\dots,p_nq1​,…,qn​,p1​,…,pn​ around it in which ω=∑idqi∧dpi\symp=\sum_i\dd q_i\wedge\dd p_iω=∑i​dqi​∧dpi​. (da Silva, §8.1; Arnold, §43.)

Such a chart is a Darboux chart, or canonical coordinates. So any statement about ω\sympω alone — or about the bracket and the fields Xf\hvf{f}Xf​ built from it — that is proved in qqq’s and ppp’s holds near every point of every symplectic manifold.

What “no local invariants” means — and what it does not

Compare a Riemannian metric, which measures lengths and angles. A sphere of radius RRR has curvature 1/R21/R^{2}1/R2 at every point, and curvature is a local invariant: no chart, however small, makes the sphere’s metric into the flat dx2+dy2\dd x^{2}+\dd y^{2}dx2+dy2. Darboux’s theorem says a symplectic form has nothing of the kind (Figure 3.2): every small patch of every 2n2n2n-dimensional symplectic manifold is indistinguishable from every other, and the dimension is the only local invariant there is.

It is easy to hear “no local invariants” as “nothing interesting happens”, and that is the opposite of the point: everything interesting is global. It lives in loops that do not bound, in regions of finite size, in how charts are glued together — never at a point. The actions of Lecture 5 are integrals over loops, and the tori of Lecture 4 are compact; neither is visible in a Darboux chart.

Why it is true: Moser’s idea

At a single point, linear algebra already makes ω\sympω standard (the reading proves this). Call that constant form ω0\symp_0ω0​ and join it to ω\sympω by the straight line ωt=ω0+t(ω−ω0)\symp_t=\symp_0+t(\symp-\symp_0)ωt​=ω0​+t(ω−ω0​), 0≤t≤10\le t\le10≤t≤1. Near the point each ωt\symp_tωt​ is non-degenerate, and ω−ω0\symp-\symp_0ω−ω0​ is closed, hence ω−ω0=dσ\symp-\symp_0=\dd\sigmaω−ω0​=dσ by the Poincaré lemma (Theorem 2.15). Now look for a flow ψt\psi_tψt​ that pulls every ωt\symp_tωt​ back to ω0\symp_0ω0​. Its velocity VtV_tVt​ is forced: ιVtωt=−σ\iota_{V_t}\symp_t=-\sigmaιVt​​ωt​=−σ, which non-degeneracy solves. That this VtV_tVt​ does the job is one differentiation, which uses dωt=0\dd\symp_t=0dωt​=0 and a formula for differentiating a form along a flow that we cite (reading). Then ψ1\psi_1ψ1​ carries ω\sympω to ω0\symp_0ω0​, and its coordinates are a Darboux chart.

At a point it is linear algebra; near a point it is Moser

Lemma 3.11 (Linear Darboux). Let ω\sympω be a non-degenerate antisymmetric bilinear form on a vector space VVV. Then VVV has a basis e1,…,en,f1,…,fne_1,\dots,e_n,f_1,\dots,f_ne1​,…,en​,f1​,…,fn​ with ω(ei,fj)=δij\symp(e_i,f_j)=\delta_{ij}ω(ei​,fj​)=δij​ and ω(ei,ej)=ω(fi,fj)=0\symp(e_i,e_j)=\symp(f_i,f_j)=0ω(ei​,ej​)=ω(fi​,fj​)=0. On U=span⁡(e1,f1)U=\Span(e_1,f_1)U=span(e1​,f1​) the form is non-degenerate, and its ω\sympω-complement Uω={v:ω(v,e1)=ω(v,f1)=0}U^{\symp}=\{v:\symp(v,e_1)=\symp(v,f_1)=0\}Uω={v:ω(v,e1​)=ω(v,f1​)=0} has dimension dim⁡V−2\dim V-2dimV−2 and meets UUU only in 000. So V=U⊕UωV=U\oplus U^{\symp}V=U⊕Uω, and ω\sympω is still non-degenerate on UωU^{\symp}Uω: a vector there pairing to zero with all of UωU^{\symp}Uω also pairs to zero with UUU, hence with VVV. Repeat inside UωU^{\symp}Uω. 

Lemma 3.11 makes ω\sympω standard at one point by a linear change of coordinates. A metric can be pushed a little further — suitable coordinates make it Euclidean at a point to first order — but no further: at second order its curvature is in the way. A symplectic form can be made standard on a whole neighbourhood, and that is Theorem 3.10. The proof spends closedness in exactly one place.

Proof of Theorem 3.10 (sketch: Moser’s trick) (★). Work in a chart around a point z0z_0z0​ in which, by Lemma 3.11, ω1:=ω\symp_1:=\sympω1​:=ω agrees at z0z_0z0​ with the constant form ω0=∑dqi∧dpi\symp_0=\sum\dd q_i\wedge\dd p_iω0​=∑dqi​∧dpi​. Join them by ωt=ω0+t(ω1−ω0)\symp_t=\symp_0+t(\symp_1-\symp_0)ωt​=ω0​+t(ω1​−ω0​), t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]t∈[0,1]. Each ωt\symp_tωt​ is closed, and equals ω0\symp_0ω0​ at z0z_0z0​, so it is non-degenerate on a small ball around z0z_0z0​. The use Lectures 4 and 5 make of it

Theorem 3.12 (Darboux, adapted to commuting functions cited). Let F1,…,FnF_1,\dots,F_nF1​,…,Fn​ be functions with {Fi,Fj}=0\pb{F_i}{F_j}=0{Fi​,Fj​}=0 and dF1,…,dFn\dd F_1,\dots,\dd F_ndF1​,…,dFn​ linearly independent at a point. Near that point there are functions ψ1,…,ψn\psi_1,\dots,\psi_nψ1​,…,ψn​ such that (ψ,F)(\psi,F)(ψ,F) is a Darboux chart: ω=∑idψi∧dFi\symp=\sum_i\dd\psi_i\wedge\dd F_iω=∑i​dψi​∧dFi​. (Bolsinov–Fomenko, Lemma 1.1, stated there in their convention ω=∑dp∧dq\symp=\sum\dd p\wedge\dd qω=∑dp∧dq.)

In such a chart the FiF_iFi​ are momenta and the ψi\psi_iψi​ positions, so by Proposition 3.6 XFj=∂/∂ψj\hvf{F_j}=\partial/\partial\psi_jXFj​​=∂/∂ψj​: the commuting flows are translations at unit speed. That is the whole of the Liouville–Arnold theorem locally, and it costs nothing — as Babelon, Bernard and Talon remark (ch. 2, Remark 2), near any point where dH≠0\dd H\ne0dH=0 Darboux gives canonical coordinates with H=P1H=P_1H=P1​, so every Hamiltonian is “integrable” on a small enough patch.

So Lecture 4 is not trivial. Its question is whether the ψi\psi_iψi​ continue over a whole level set, and what they do when they are continued: they come back to themselves, which makes them angles and the level set a torus. Action-angle coordinates are an adapted Darboux chart on a whole neighbourhood of a torus, and the global part is what Lectures 4 and 5 add.

3.4 Canonical transformations and generating functions

Definition 3.13 (Symplectomorphism). A diffeomorphism F ⁣:(M,ω)→(M′,ω′)F\colon(\phase,\symp)\to(\phase',\symp')F:(M,ω)→(M′,ω′) is a symplectomorphism if F∗ω′=ωF^{*}\symp'=\sympF∗ω′=ω.

Generating functions

A transformation given as a formula is easy to check. The problem in practice runs the other way: to produce canonical transformations adapted to a given HHH. Generating functions do this, and the form language says in one line why they work.

Proposition 3.16 (Why generating functions work). Let S(q,P)S(q,P)S(q,P) be a function of nnn old positions and nnn new momenta, and define (q,p)↦(Q,P)(q,p)\mapsto(Q,P)(q,p)↦(Q,P) implicitly by pi=∂S∂qi,Qi=∂S∂Pi, p_i=\frac{\partial S}{\partial q_i}, \qquad Q_i=\frac{\partial S}{\partial P_i}, pi​=∂qi​∂S​,Qi​=∂Pi​∂S​,(3.10) wherever (q,P)(q,P)(q,P) are good coordinates. Then (3.9) holds.

Proof. In the coordinates (q,P)(q,P)(q,P), (3.10) says exactly that ∑ipi dqi+∑iQi dPi  =  dS.\sum_i p_i\,\dd q_i+\sum_i Q_i\,\dd P_i\;=\;\dd S .i∑​pi​dqi​+i∑​Qi​dPi​=dS. Apply d\ddd. The right-hand side gives ddS=0\dd\dd S=0ddS=0 (Theorem 2.13); the left gives ∑dpi∧dqi+∑dQi∧dPi\sum\dd p_i\wedge\dd q_i+\sum\dd Q_i\wedge\dd P_i∑dpi​∧dqi​+∑dQi​∧dPi​. So ∑dQi∧dPi=−∑dpi∧dqi=∑dqi∧dpi\sum\dd Q_i\wedge\dd P_i=-\sum\dd p_i\wedge\dd q_i=\sum\dd q_i\wedge\dd p_i∑dQi​∧dPi​=−∑dpi​∧dqi​=∑dqi​∧dpi​. 

That is the mechanism in full: a generating function is a primitive for a combination of canonical 111-forms, and d∘d=0\dd\circ\dd=0d∘d=0 turns “exact” into “canonical”. For example S=∑iqiPi+f(q)S=\sum_iq_iP_i+f(q)S=∑i​qi​Pi​+f(q) gives Q=qQ=qQ=q and P=p−∇fP=p-\nabla fP=p−∇f: shifting every momentum by a gradient is canonical. The function ∑iqiPi\sum_i q_iP_i∑i​qi​Pi​ alone gives the identity.

The other classical types work identically. A type-1 function S(q,Q)S(q,Q)S(q,Q) with p=∂S/∂qp=\partial S/\partial qp=∂S/∂q and P=−∂S/∂QP=-\partial S/\partial QP=−∂S/∂Q says p⋅dq−P⋅dQ=dSp\cdot\dd q-P\cdot\dd Q=\dd Sp⋅dq−P⋅dQ=dS; for instance S=qQS=qQS=qQ gives (Q,P)=(p,−q)(Q,P)=(p,-q)(Q,P)=(p,−q), which exchanges position and momentum up to a sign. Type 1 cannot generate the identity, whose qqq and QQQ are not independent, which is one reason type 2 is the workhorse and the type Lecture 5 uses.

Hamilton–Jacobi, recalled in this language

Hamilton–Jacobi looks for a type-2 generating function adapted to HHH: an S(q,P)S(q,P)S(q,P) with H(q,∂S∂q)=K(P) H\Big(q,\frac{\partial S}{\partial q}\Big)=K(P) H(q,∂q∂S​)=K(P)(3.11) for some function KKK of the new momenta alone. Proposition 3.17 (The Liouville volume form). In canonical coordinates, ωnn!=dq1∧dp1∧dq2∧dp2∧⋯∧dqn∧dpn, \frac{\symp^{n}}{n!} =\dd q_1\wedge\dd p_1\wedge\dd q_2\wedge\dd p_2\wedge\cdots\wedge\dd q_n\wedge\dd p_n , n!ωn​=dq1​∧dp1​∧dq2​∧dp2​∧⋯∧dqn​∧dpn​,(3.12) which as a measure is Lecture 1’s phase-space volume dq1⋯dqn dp1⋯dpn\dd q_1\cdots\dd q_n\,\dd p_1\cdots\dd p_ndq1​⋯dqn​dp1​⋯dpn​. For n=1n=1n=1 this is Liouville again; for n≥2n\ge2n≥2 it conserves the sum of the signed areas of the loop’s nnn shadows, counted with winding number (a figure-eight shadow contributes the difference of its lobes), not a volume. Theorem 3.20 (Gromov non-squeezing cited). A symplectomorphism can map a ball of radius rrr in R2n\R^{2n}R2n into the cylinder {q12+p12<R2}\{q_1^{2}+p_1^{2}<R^{2}\}{q12​+p12​<R2} only if r≤Rr\le Rr≤R. (Gromov, Invent. Math. 82, 1985.)

For n≥2n\ge2n≥2 the cylinder has infinite volume, so this is symplectic, not volumetric — and not local, since it concerns a ball of definite size. We shall not use it.

3.6 Lagrangian submanifolds

How large can a subspace be on which ω\sympω vanishes?

Let dim⁡V=2n\dim V=2ndimV=2n with ω\sympω non-degenerate. The ω\sympω-complement of a subspace UUU is Uω={v:ω(v,u)=0 for all u∈U}U^{\symp}=\{v:\symp(v,u)=0\text{ for all }u\in U\}Uω={v:ω(v,u)=0 for all u∈U}; by (3.1) it is the preimage of the covectors vanishing on UUU, so dim⁡Uω=2n−dim⁡U. \dim U^{\symp}=2n-\dim U . dimUω=2n−dimU.(3.13) Unlike an orthogonal complement, UωU^{\symp}Uω can contain UUU, since every vector is ω\sympω-orthogonal to itself. Call UUU isotropic if ω\sympω vanishes on it, i.e. U⊆UωU\subseteq U^{\symp}U⊆Uω; then (3.13) gives dim⁡U≤2n−dim⁡U\dim U\le 2n-\dim UdimU≤2n−dimU: an isotropic subspace has dimension at most nnn.

Definition 3.21 (Lagrangian subspace, Lagrangian submanifold). A Lagrangian subspace is an isotropic subspace of the maximal dimension nnn. A submanifold L⊂ML\subset\phaseL⊂M is Lagrangian if it has dimension nnn and ω(v,w)=0\symp(v,w)=0ω(v,w)=0 for all v,wv,wv,w tangent to LLL — equivalently, if the pullback of ω\sympω to LLL vanishes, written ω∣L=0\symp|_{L}=0ω∣L​=0.

This bound is why Lecture 4 asks for exactly nnn integrals.

Proposition 3.22 (At most nnn commuting integrals). If F1,…,FkF_1,\dots,F_kF1​,…,Fk​ satisfy {Fi,Fj}=0\pb{F_i}{F_j}=0{Fi​,Fj​}=0 and dF1,…,dFk\dd F_1,\dots,\dd F_kdF1​,…,dFk​ are linearly independent at a point, then k≤nk\le nk≤n.

Proof. At that point the vectors XFi\hvf{F_i}XFi​​ are linearly independent, since ιXFiω=dFi\iota_{\hvf{F_i}}\symp=\dd F_iιXFi​​​ω=dFi​ and v↦ιvωv\mapsto\iota_v\sympv↦ιv​ω is an isomorphism. They span an isotropic subspace, since ω(XFi,XFj)={Fi,Fj}=0\symp(\hvf{F_i},\hvf{F_j})=\pb{F_i}{F_j}=0ω(XFi​​,XFj​​)={Fi​,Fj​}=0 by (3.6). So k≤nk\le nk≤n. 

Seeing it in R4\R^{4}R4

In R4\R^{4}R4, ω(v,w)=A1+A2\symp(v,w)=A_1+A_2ω(v,w)=A1​+A2​, the signed areas of the two shadows of the parallelogram on v,wv,wv,w. A plane is Lagrangian when the two shadow areas of a basis parallelogram cancel (Figure 3.5).

Examples

Example 3.23 (Curves in the plane). For n=1n=1n=1 every curve is Lagrangian: it has dimension 1=n1=n1=n, and a 222-form vanishes on parallel vectors. The notion has content from n=2n=2n=2 on.

Example 3.24 (Positions and momenta). In R2n\R^{2n}R2n the qqq-space {p=0}\{p=0\}{p=0} and each ppp-space {q=const}\{q=\text{const}\}{q=const} are Lagrangian, since ω\sympω pairs a qqq-direction only with a ppp-direction. The (q1,p1)(q_1,p_1)(q1​,p1​)-plane is not: ω\sympω restricts to dq1∧dp1\dd q_1\wedge\dd p_1dq1​∧dp1​ on it.

The most important examples are graphs, and they bring back Lecture 2.

In particular the graph of dS\dd SdS, pi=∂S∂qi, p_i=\frac{\partial S}{\partial q_i}, pi​=∂qi​∂S​,(3.14) is Lagrangian for every function SSS.

Proof. Parametrise LσL_\sigmaLσ​ by qqq. Pulling back is substituting pi=σi(q)p_i=\sigma_i(q)pi​=σi​(q): ω∣Lσ=∑idqi∧dσi=∑i,j∂σi∂qj dqi∧dqj=−∑i,j∂σi∂qj dqj∧dqi=−dσ,\symp|_{L_\sigma}=\sum_i\dd q_i\wedge\dd\sigma_i =\sum_{i,j}\frac{\partial\sigma_i}{\partial q_j}\,\dd q_i\wedge\dd q_j =-\sum_{i,j}\frac{\partial\sigma_i}{\partial q_j}\,\dd q_j\wedge\dd q_i =-\dd\sigma ,ω∣Lσ​​=i∑​dqi​∧dσi​=i,j∑​∂qj​∂σi​​dqi​∧dqj​=−i,j∑​∂qj​∂σi​​dqj​∧dqi​=−dσ, by (2.6) and (2.10). For σ=dS\sigma=\dd Sσ=dS this vanishes by Theorem 2.13. 

SSS is called a generating function of the Lagrangian submanifold, and the name is not a coincidence: by (3.11), a solution of Hamilton–Jacobi is a family of Lagrangian graphs, one for each value of PPP, each lying in a level set of HHH. Lecture 5’s S(q,I)S(q,I)S(q,I) is exactly that, with the invariant tori as the family.

Reading

By the Poincaré lemma a closed σ\sigmaσ is locally some dS\dd SdS; globally it need not be. On the pendulum’s cylinder, with angle qqq, a rotation orbit at energy E>1E>1E>1 is the graph p=2(E+cos⁡q)p=\sqrt{2(E+\cos q)}p=2(E+cosq)​ of the 111-form σ=2(E+cos⁡q) dq\sigma=\sqrt{2(E+\cos q)}\,\dd qσ=2(E+cosq)​dq — closed, as every 111-form on a circle is, and Lagrangian. It is not dS\dd SdS for any function SSS on the circle, for the reason of Proposition 2.17: ∮σ>0\oint\sigma>0∮σ>0. Lecture 5 calls 12π∮σ\frac{1}{2\pi}\oint\sigma2π1​∮σ the rotating pendulum’s action. A nonzero action is precisely the obstruction to a global generating function, and Lecture 5 lives in that gap.

Example 3.26 (A Lagrangian torus in R4\R^{4}R4). Take the two-dimensional oscillator’s integrals Fi=12(qi2+pi2)F_i=\tfrac12(q_i^{2}+p_i^{2})Fi​=21​(qi2​+pi2​) and, for c1,c2>0c_1,c_2>0c1​,c2​>0, the level set T={F1=c1, F2=c2}={q12+p12=2c1}×{q22+p22=2c2},T=\{F_1=c_1,\ F_2=c_2\} =\{q_1^{2}+p_1^{2}=2c_1\}\times\{q_2^{2}+p_2^{2}=2c_2\},T={F1​=c1​, F2​=c2​}={q12​+p12​=2c1​}×{q22​+p22​=2c2​}, a circle in each symplectic plane: a torus (Figure 3.7). Its tangent spaces are spanned by XF1=p1∂q1−q1∂p1\hvf{F_1}=p_1\partial_{q_1}-q_1\partial_{p_1}XF1​​=p1​∂q1​​−q1​∂p1​​ and XF2=p2∂q2−q2∂p2\hvf{F_2}=p_2\partial_{q_2}-q_2\partial_{p_2}XF2​​=p2​∂q2​​−q2​∂p2​​, each tangent to its own circle and nonzero there, and ω(XF1,XF2)={F1,F2}=0\symp(\hvf{F_1},\hvf{F_2})=\pb{F_1}{F_2}=0ω(XF1​​,XF2​​)={F1​,F2​}=0. So TTT is Lagrangian: each tangent parallelogram has one edge in each symplectic plane, so both its shadows are degenerate.

Example 3.26 is Lecture 4’s first proof step, done by hand; the general argument is Proposition 3.22’s, with equality. Like the circle of Figure 3.6, TTT is not a graph over (q1,q2)(q_1,q_2)(q1​,q2​).

3.7 Cotangent bundles and the canonical 111-form

Positions and their momenta

Let Q\configQ be a configuration space, a manifold of dimension nnn — the circle for the pendulum, the torus T2T^{2}T2 for the double pendulum. Its cotangent bundle is the set of pairs T∗Q={(q,p): q∈Q, p∈Tq∗Q},π(q,p)=q,T^{*}\config=\{(q,p):\ q\in\config,\ p\in T^{*}_{q}\config\}, \qquad \pi(q,p)=q ,T∗Q={(q,p): q∈Q, p∈Tq∗​Q},π(q,p)=q, a point of configuration space and a covector there. A chart q1,…,qnq_1,\dots,q_nq1​,…,qn​ on Q\configQ writes the covector as p=∑ipi dqip=\sum_ip_i\,\dd q_ip=∑i​pi​dqi​ (Definition 2.1), and (q,p)(q,p)(q,p) is then a chart on the 2n2n2n-dimensional T∗QT^{*}\configT∗Q. That momenta are covectors shows in a change of chart q′=ϕ(q)q'=\phi(q)q′=ϕ(q): writing the same covector in both bases, ∑jpj′ dqj′=∑ipi dqi\sum_j p'_j\,\dd q'_j=\sum_i p_i\,\dd q_i∑j​pj′​dqj′​=∑i​pi​dqi​, forces pi=∑jpj′ ∂qj′∂qi: p_i=\sum_j p'_j\,\frac{\partial q'_j}{\partial q_i} : pi​=j∑​pj′​∂qi​∂qj′​​:(3.15) momenta transform like the components of a gradient, not like those of a velocity. For polar coordinates on the plane, (3.15) gives pr=(x px+y py)/rp_r=(x\,p_x+y\,p_y)/rpr​=(xpx​+ypy​)/r and pθ=x py−y pxp_\theta=x\,p_y-y\,p_xpθ​=xpy​−ypx​ — the momentum conjugate to the angle is the angular momentum, as it should be.

The canonical 111-form

Definition 3.27 (Canonical 111-form). At a point (q,p)(q,p)(q,p) of T∗QT^{*}\configT∗Q and for a tangent vector vvv there, (p⋅dq)(q,p)(v)  =  p(dπ v). (p\cdot\dd q)_{(q,p)}(v)\;=\;p\big(\dd\pi\,v\big) . (p⋅dq)(q,p)​(v)=p(dπv).(3.16) In words: push vvv down to configuration space, and feed it to the covector ppp — which is part of the point, and so is already there (Figure 3.8).

In a chart, dπ v=∑ivqi∂qi\dd\pi\,v=\sum_iv^{q_i}\partial_{q_i}dπv=∑i​vqi​∂qi​​ drops the momentum components of vvv, so (3.16) is (∑ipi dqi)(v)\big(\sum_ip_i\,\dd q_i\big)(v)(∑i​pi​dqi​)(v). The form of Example 2.4, and of Lecture 5’s action integral, is therefore the same 111-form in every cotangent chart, because (3.16) mentions no chart.

Theorem 3.28 (Every cotangent bundle is symplectic). ω=−d(p⋅dq)\symp=-\dd(p\cdot\dd q)ω=−d(p⋅dq) is a symplectic form on T∗QT^{*}\configT∗Q, and in every cotangent chart it is ∑idqi∧dpi\sum_i\dd q_i\wedge\dd p_i∑i​dqi​∧dpi​.

Proof. In a chart, d(∑ipi dqi)=∑idpi∧dqi=−∑idqi∧dpi\dd\big(\sum_ip_i\,\dd q_i\big)=\sum_i\dd p_i\wedge\dd q_i =-\sum_i\dd q_i\wedge\dd p_id(∑i​pi​dqi​)=∑i​dpi​∧dqi​=−∑i​dqi​∧dpi​, so ω\sympω is the standard form there, which is non-degenerate (Example 3.3). It is closed because it is exact: dω=−dd(p⋅dq)=0\dd\symp=-\dd\dd(p\cdot\dd q)=0dω=−dd(p⋅dq)=0. And it is the same form in every chart, because p⋅dqp\cdot\dd qp⋅dq is. 

So the pendulum’s cylinder, the double pendulum’s T∗T2T^{*}T^{2}T∗T2 and the rigid body’s T∗SO(3)T^{*}SO(3)T∗SO(3) are symplectic, with no choice made; and Poincaré’s integral invariant holds on any cotangent bundle, since its proof used only d(p⋅dq)=−ω\dd(p\cdot\dd q)=-\sympd(p⋅dq)=−ω and ιXHω=dH\iota_{\hvf{H}}\symp=\dd HιXH​​ω=dH.

The minus sign, and why it costs nothing

The minus sign in ω=−d(p⋅dq)\symp=-\dd(p\cdot\dd q)ω=−d(p⋅dq) is forced by the wedge order dq∧dp\dd q\wedge\dd pdq∧dp, which (3.4) showed is the one giving Hamilton’s equations. Sources that write ω=dp∧dq\symp=\dd p\wedge\dd qω=dp∧dq print ω=d(p dq)\symp=\dd(p\,\dd q)ω=d(pdq); do not transcribe them.

The minus is compensated where it matters. For the oscillator H=12(p2+ν2q2)H=\tfrac12(p^{2}+\freq^{2}q^{2})H=21​(p2+ν2q2), p˙=−ν2q\dot p=-\freq^{2}qp˙​=−ν2q, so at (q,p)=(1,0)(q,p)=(1,0)(q,p)=(1,0) the motion is straight down: orbits in the (q,p)(q,p)(q,p)-plane run clockwise. A clockwise orbit γ\gammaγ is the boundary of the enclosed disc DDD with the opposite of the orientation that dq∧dp\dd q\wedge\dd pdq∧dp gives it, so by Stokes ∮γp dq=−∫Dd(p dq)=+∫Dω=area of D=2πEν>0.\oint_{\gamma}p\,\dd q=-\int_D\dd(p\,\dd q)=+\int_D\symp =\text{area of }D=\frac{2\pi E}{\freq}>0 .∮γ​pdq=−∫D​d(pdq)=+∫D​ω=area of D=ν2πE​>0. Two minus signs, one from the wedge order and one from the direction of motion, and the action integral of Lecture 5, taken along the motion, comes out positive.

Point transformations are canonical

A diffeomorphism ϕ\phiϕ of configuration space moves momenta by the transpose of its inverse Jacobian — that is (3.15) read as a map — and so lifts to a map ϕ^(q,p)=(ϕ(q),p′)\hat\phi(q,p)=(\phi(q),p')ϕ^​(q,p)=(ϕ(q),p′) of T∗QT^{*}\configT∗Q, the cotangent lift. Because p⋅dqp\cdot\dd qp⋅dq is defined without a chart, ϕ^∗(p⋅dq)=p⋅dq\hat\phi^{*}(p\cdot\dd q)=p\cdot\dd qϕ^​∗(p⋅dq)=p⋅dq, and hence ϕ^∗ω=ω\hat\phi^{*}\symp=\sympϕ^​∗ω=ω by (2.15). Every change of configuration coordinates, with the momenta carried along as covectors, is a canonical transformation. This is why passing to polar coordinates, with pθp_\thetapθ​ the angular momentum, never needs checking. It is also the type-2 generating function S(q,p′)=∑jpj′ ϕj(q)S(q,p')=\sum_jp'_j\,\phi_j(q)S(q,p′)=∑j​pj′​ϕj​(q) of Proposition 3.16, as a one-line computation with (3.10) confirms.

Summary

  • The structure. A closed, non-degenerate 222-form (Definition 3.2); non-degeneracy turns covectors into vectors (3.1) and forces even dimension (Proposition 3.4). The standard form is ∑dqi∧dpi\sum\dd q_i\wedge\dd p_i∑dqi​∧dpi​, in that order, because that order gives Hamilton’s equations (3.4).
  • One structure. ιXfω=df\iota_{\hvf{f}}\symp=\dd fιXf​​ω=df recovers Lecture 1’s Xf\hvf{f}Xf​, with ω(Xf,Xg)={f,g}\symp(\hvf{f},\hvf{g})=\pb{f}{g}ω(Xf​,Xg​)={f,g} (Proposition 3.6), and the bracket satisfies Jacobi exactly when dω=0\dd\symp=0dω=0 (Theorem 3.8).
  • Darboux. Locally every symplectic manifold is standard (Theorem 3.10), even with nnn given commuting functions as momenta (Theorem 3.12). Everything interesting is global.
  • Canonical transformations are the symplectomorphisms; Hamiltonian flows are among them (Proposition 3.15); generating functions work because d∘d=0\dd\circ\dd=0d∘d=0 (Proposition 3.16). The flow preserves the volume ωn/n!\symp^{n}/n!ωn/n! and Poincaré’s ∮p⋅dq\oint p\cdot\dd q∮p⋅dq (Theorems 3.18 and 3.19).
  • Lagrangian submanifolds: dimension nnn, ω∣L=0\symp|_L=0ω∣L​=0. At most nnn independent functions commute (Proposition 3.22); graphs of dS\dd SdS and the oscillator torus are Lagrangian (Proposition 3.25, Example 3.26).
  • Cotangent bundles are symplectic for free, with ω=−d(p⋅dq)\symp=-\dd(p\cdot\dd q)ω=−d(p⋅dq) (Theorem 3.28): the minus is forced by the wedge order and cancelled by the clockwise motion of orbits.
